quotes.t: Non-cooperation with evil is as much a duty as is cooperation with good.
A small body of determined spirits fired by an unquenchable faith in their mission can alter the course of history.
In matters of conscience, the law of majority has no place.
All women become like their mothers. That is their tragedy. No man does. That's his.
There is no sin except stupidity.
A man can be happy with any woman, as long as he does not love her.
Personally, I'm always ready to learn, although I do not always like being taught.
Kites rise highest against the wind, not with it.
It is no use saying, 'We are doing our best.' You have got to succeed in doing what is necessary.
In a word, literature is my Utopia. Here I am not disfranchised. No barrier of the senses shuts me out from the sweet, gracious discourse of my book-friends.
I thank God for my handicaps, for through them, I have found myself, my work, and my God.
No one has a right to consume happiness without producing it.
When you cannot be deceived by men you will have realized the wisdom of strategy.
The primary thing when you take a sword in your hands is your intention to cut the enemy, whatever the means.
When you have mastered the Way of strategy you can suddenly make your body like a rock, and ten thousand things cannot touch you.
The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.
He will win whose army is animated by the same spirit throughout all its ranks.
Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.
Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.
quotes.source: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

quotes.t: Anything that makes weak — physically, intellectually and spiritually, reject it as poison.
quotes.source: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

quotes.t: We reap what we sow. We are the makers of our own fate.
quotes.source: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda

quotes.t: Patience serves as a protection against wrongs as clothes do against cold.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: He who can go to the fountain does not go to the water-jar.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: It is easier to resist at the beginning than at the end.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: Thinking is progress. Non-thinking is stagnation of the individual, organisation and the country.
Be more dedicated to making solid achievements than in running after swift but synthetic happiness.

If a country is to be corruption free and become a nation of beautiful minds, I strongly feel there are three key societal members who can make a difference. They are the father, the mother and the teacher.
What I know for sure is that speaking your truth is the most powerful tool we all have.
When I look into the future, it's so bright it burns my eyes.
The thing you fear most has no power. Your fear of it is what has the power. Facing the truth really will set you free.

Surely, in the light of history, it is more intelligent to hope rather than to fear, to try rather than not to try. For one thing we know beyond all doubt: Nothing has ever been achieved by the person who says, 'It can't be done.'
You have to accept whatever comes, and the only important thing is that you meet it with the best you have to give.
The most important thing in any relationship is not what you get but what you give.
A consistent man believes in destiny, a capricious man in chance.

A great city, whose image dwells in the memory of man, is the type of some great idea. Rome represents conquest; Faith hovers over the towers of Jerusalem; and Athens embodies the pre-eminent quality of the antique world, Art.
I repeat that all power is a trust; that we are accountable for its exercise; that from the people, and for the people all springs, and all must exist.
Whoever does not have two-thirds of his day for himself, is a slave, whatever he may be: a statesman, a businessman, an official, or a scholar.
One must pay dearly for immortality; one has to die several times while still alive.
He who would learn to fly one day must first learn to stand and walk and run and climb and dance; one cannot fly into flying.
Never, never, and never again shall it be that this beautiful land will again experience the oppression of one by another.
Like slavery and apartheid, poverty is not natural. It is man-made and it can be overcome and eradicated by the actions of human beings.
quotes.source: Make Poverty History rally, Trafalgar Square, 3 February 2005

quotes.t: Sometimes it falls upon a generation to be great. You can be that great generation.
quotes.source: Make Poverty History rally, Trafalgar Square, 3 February 2005

quotes.t: The strength of a man's virtue must not be measured by his efforts, but by his ordinary life.
The greater intellect one has, the more originality one finds in men. Ordinary persons find no difference between men.
We do not content ourselves with the life we have in ourselves and in our own being; we desire to live an imaginary life in the mind of others, and for this purpose we endeavour to shine.
I can hardly understand the importance given to the word research in connection with modern painting. In my opinion to search means nothing in painting. To find is the thing.
Colors, like features, follow the changes of the emotions.
Painting is a blind man's profession. He paints not what he sees, but what he feels, what he tells himself about what he has seen.

We need to find God, and he cannot be found in noise and restlessness. God is the friend of silence. See how nature — trees, flowers, grass — grows in silence; see the stars, the moon and the sun, how they move in silence. We need silence to be able to touch souls.
It is not how much we do, but how much love we put in the doing. It is not how much we give, but how much love we put in the giving.
The first requirement for prayer is silence. People of prayer are people of silence.
quotes.source: Mother Teresa: In My Own Words

quotes.t: Winter is on my head, but eternal spring is in my heart.

The power of a glance has been so much abused in love stories, that it has come to be disbelieved in. Few people dare now to say that two beings have fallen in love because they have looked at each other. Yet it is in this way that love begins, and in this way only.
Those who do not weep, do not see.
The absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.
This whole thing is not about heroism. It's about decency. It may seem a ridiculous idea, but the only way to fight the plague is with decency.
I leave Sisyphus at the foot of the mountain! One always finds one's burden again.
If everyone demanded peace instead of another television set, then there'd be peace.
We're trying to sell peace, like a product, you know, and sell it like people sell soap or soft drinks.
You feel alone if you're the only one thinking 'wouldn't it be nice if there was peace and nobody was getting killed.' So advertise yourself that you're for peace if you believe in it.
The liar's punishment is, not in the least that he is not believed, but that he cannot believe anyone else.
There is no greater evil than men's failure to consult and to consider.
I am life that wills to live in the midst of life that wills to live.
quotes.source: Out of My Life and Thought

quotes.t: I am sometimes a fox, but I know how to be a lion.

The most fundamental aggression to ourselves, the most fundamental harm we can do to ourselves, is to remain ignorant by not having the courage and the respect to look at ourselves honestly and gently.
The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways — I to die, and you to live. Which is better God only knows.
Learning is like rowing upstream; not to advance is to drop back.
The cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run.
Life and death are of supreme importance. Time swiftly passes by and opportunity is lost. Each of us should strive to awaken. Awaken! Take heed, do not squander your life.
The only alternative to coexistence is codestruction.
Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, cities will never have rest from their evils.
Let us work without theorizing; 'tis the only way to make life endurable.
The quality, not the longevity, of one's life is what is important.
Tell all the truth but tell it slant — Success in Circuit lies
My advice is, never do tomorrow what you can do today. Procrastination is the thief of time. Collar him!
He that is good for making excuses is seldom good for anything else.
I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
The truth is obtained like gold, not by letting it grow bigger, but by washing off from it everything that isn't gold.
Suffering is the sole origin of consciousness.
I don't think of all the misery, but of the beauty that still remains.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: I am human because I belong, I participate, I share.
Each friend represents a world in us, a world possibly not born until they arrive, and it is only by this meeting that a new world is born.
It is a bad plan that admits of no modification.
Music is well said to be the speech of angels.
So long as you write what you wish to write, that is all that matters; and whether it matters for ages or only for hours, nobody can say.
Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?
quotes.source: The Summer Day, in House of Light (1990)

quotes.t: After the final no there comes a yes.
quotes.source: The Well Dressed Man with a Beard, in Parts of a World (1942)

quotes.t: The art of losing isn't hard to master.
We wear the mask that grins and lies.
quotes.source: We Wear the Mask, in Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896)

quotes.t: If we must die, let it not be like hogs.
quotes.source: If We Must Die, in The Liberator (1919)

quotes.t: Yet do I marvel at this curious thing: to make a poet black, and bid him sing!
quotes.source: Yet Do I Marvel, in Color (1925)

quotes.t: Lift every voice and sing, till earth and heaven ring.
There are wrongs which even the grave does not bury.
quotes.source: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861)

quotes.t: Reading is to the mind, what exercise is to the body.
All art constantly aspires towards the condition of music.
quotes.source: The School of Giorgione, in The Renaissance (1877)

quotes.t: I am—yet what I am none cares or knows.
quotes.source: I Am, first published in the Bedford Times (1848)

quotes.t: Your enjoyment of the world is never right, till every morning you awake in Heaven.
quotes.source: Centuries of Meditations, First Century, Meditation 28 (published 1908)

quotes.t: I felt my legs were praying.
quotes.source: Written account of the Selma to Montgomery march (1965)

quotes.t: Don't ask yourself what the world needs. Ask yourself what makes you come alive, and go do that, because what the world needs is people who have come alive.
quotes.source: As recalled by Gil Bailie, Violence Unveiled (1995)

quotes.t: People say, what is the sense of our small effort? They cannot see that we must lay one brick at a time, take one step at a time.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Abraham Joshua Heschel.bio: Polish-born American rabbi and theologian (1907–1972), a leading Jewish thinker and civil rights ally of Martin Luther King Jr.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Claude McKay.bio: Jamaican-born American poet and novelist, a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

Countee Cullen.bio: American poet (1903–1946), a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance; his first collection, Color, appeared in 1925.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Dorothy Day.bio: American journalist and social activist (1897–1980), co-founder of the Catholic Worker Movement in 1933.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Elizabeth Bishop.bio: American poet (1911–1979) who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1956 and the National Book Award in 1970.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Harriet Jacobs.bio: American abolitionist and writer (1813–1897), author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861), the first full-length narrative by a Black woman published in the United States.

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Howard Thurman.bio: American theologian and civil rights leader (1899–1981), author of Jesus and the Disinherited (1949), whose work influenced Martin Luther King Jr.

James Weldon Johnson.bio: American writer and civil rights leader (1871–1938), executive secretary of the NAACP and lyricist of Lift Every Voice and Sing.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Clare.bio: English poet (1793–1864), known as the peasant poet for his poems of rural life and nature.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Joseph Addison.bio: English essayist, poet and politician (1672–1719), co-founder of The Spectator magazine.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Oliver.bio: American poet (1935–2019) who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984 and the National Book Award in 1992, known for her nature poetry.

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Paul Laurence Dunbar.bio: American poet and novelist (1872–1906), one of the first African American poets to gain national acclaim.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Traherne.bio: English poet and Anglican clergyman (d. 1674), author of Centuries of Meditations, first published in 1908.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Wallace Stevens.bio: American modernist poet (1879–1955), author of Harmonium and winner of the 1955 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

Walter Pater.bio: English critic and essayist (1839–1894), author of Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873) and a leading figure of the Aesthetic movement.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
